comparisons.interpretation: Valdez names social-housing institutions and tenant power; Carmona emphasizes targeted housing, enforceable anti-discrimination protections and supportive services. These strategies can coexist, and Carmona's answer does not establish rejection of public housing.
Valdez foregrounds community services and decriminalization; Carmona combines oversight and training with diversion and community-based responses. Both discuss alternatives to incarceration.
Both support the named sex-work decriminalization bill. Carmona's shorter affirmative remains an actual commitment, not a weaker or contrary stance inferred from answer length.
Both support practical and financial help for people seeking reproductive care, although they do not supply identical program designs.

Valdez foregrounds union organizing and worker power; Carmona foregrounds legal advocacy and public service. Both describe community participation, so these are differences of emphasis rather than exclusive categories.

Gallagher proposes large-scale permanent public/community housing and criticizes reliance on temporary private incentives. Simpkins proposes investment and tax incentives with labor and affordability conditions. The answer does not establish that Simpkins endorses every existing subsidy model Gallagher criticizes.
Gallagher names human-rights-law and corrections-commission bills; Simpkins names review boards, training and community reinvestment. These are potentially complementary accountability mechanisms.
Both support funding and practical assistance to remove barriers to abortion access. Gallagher identifies a specific fund; Simpkins describes broader funding and logistical support.

Gallagher singles out the social-housing authority as her biggest priority; Simpkins lists housing, education and environment. These self-stated priorities do not establish measured campaign-message frequency.
Soto proposes priority access to income-restricted apartments for marginalized groups; Benedetto proposes LGBTQ-specific housing. Allocation preferences and targeted construction can coexist.
Soto affirmatively supports the bill; Benedetto says he is open to learning more. The contrast is commitment versus an unresolved position, not a fabricated support/oppose split.
Both support removing Vice Squads in their own answers. Benedetto's uncertainty on a separate decriminalization bill does not negate this explicit answer.
Soto names a prospective school, tenant and public-renewables agenda; Benedetto foregrounds his governing record and an open-door relationship with constituents.

Both explicitly commit to protecting tenants. Zinerman supplies a particular receivership/repair mechanism; Huntley's short statement does not specify the same mechanism. Their campaign-finance conflict does not establish opposing tenant-protection goals.
